lessons.teacherScript: Hello, everyone! Last time, we said, Every one of us has a story to tell. Nib walks with us to the round exit of the Labyrinth, holding the Storybook. He waves goodbye with his little paw. Then we step outside, and wow! Green hills roll away in every direction. There are old stone walls, fluffy white sheep and fields of purple heather. Down in the valley is a little village called Heatherbrook. On the highest hill, Heart Hill, a huge rainbow hangs in the sky. The rainbow is pale and white, with no colors at all. Suddenly, a small, soft cloud floats down next to Kiko. Hello! I'm Puff, it says. Welcome to the Highlands of the Heart. How are you really feeling? Haru laughs, and the sunshine gets a little warmer. Puff explains, The weather here changes with your feelings. Say it with me. The weather here changes with your feelings. Great! Then a kind old woman in a woolly hat comes up the path with a sheepdog. She is Grandma Rowan, a shepherd, and her dog is called Biscuit. You can all stay at my farmhouse with your teacher, she says. Let's read the sign on her gate. "Welcome to the Highlands of the Heart! Here, the sky listens to your heart. When you are sad, a small rain cloud may follow you. When you feel shy or embarrassed, a pink mist may appear around you. When friends laugh together, warm sunshine pours down. And when people argue, thick fog rolls over the hills. Please don't worry. All feelings are welcome here. Long ago, people in the highlands shared their feelings every day, and the Great Rainbow above Heart Hill was full of color. Then people stopped talking about their hearts, and the colors faded. If you learn the skills of the heart, the rainbow will shine again." What happens when friends laugh together? Warm sunshine pours down. Why did the colors fade? Because people stopped talking about their hearts. Puff turns a little gray. Each time you learn a heart skill, Puff says, a color will return to the rainbow. We all promise to help. Now, phonics. Some feeling words have tricky spellings. Embarrassed has two r's and two s's. Frustrated is frus-trat-ed, with no extra e. Relieved has i before e. Next time, we'll find better words than just happy.

lessons.teacherScript: Hello, everyone! Last time, we said, The weather here changes with your feelings. This morning, we wake up in Grandma Rowan's stone farmhouse, and the kitchen smells wonderful. Grandma Rowan is making a tall stack of pancakes with golden syrup and fresh berries. Birimo takes one bite, closes his eyes and spins around the table. Bright sunshine bursts through the window. Puff floats over and asks, Birimo, how are you really feeling? Are you happy? Birimo shakes his head. Happy? Happy isn't big enough! I'm not just happy. I'm over the moon! Say it with me. I'm not just happy. I'm over the moon! Fantastic! Grandma Rowan laughs. Puff says that happy is a good word, but there are many other words that tell people exactly how you feel. Then Puff opens a little book with a fluffy cover. It's Puff's Feelings Book. Let's read the first page. "Not Just Happy. Happy is a great word, but it is only the beginning. If you are very, very happy, you can say, I'm over the moon! If you are excited about something that is happening now or very soon, you can say, I'm thrilled! If someone did something kind for you, you can say, I'm grateful. If you feel happy and calm, like a cat in the sun, you can say, I'm content. If a nice surprise makes you smile, you can say, I'm delighted. When you choose the right word, your friends can understand your heart better. So next time you feel happy, stop for a moment and ask yourself, What kind of happy is this?" What can you say when you are very, very happy? I'm over the moon! What can you say when someone did something kind for you? I'm grateful. Kiko looks up from her plate and says, Grandma Rowan, I'm grateful for your kindness. Haru adds, And I'm thrilled about exploring the hills today! The kitchen gets so sunny that Biscuit lies down in a warm square of light and starts to snore. Now, phonics. More tricky feeling words. Annoyed has two n's, and it ends in o, y, e, d. Anxious has an x, and then i, o, u, s. Disappointed is dis, plus appoint, plus ed, so it has one s and two p's. Next time, Biscuit gets into a little trouble, and we'll learn how to say how strong a feeling is.

lessons.teacherScript: Hello, everyone! Last time, we said, I'm not just happy. I'm over the moon! Today, we're helping Grandma Rowan in the farmyard. Birimo takes off his shoes and socks to walk on the grass. But when he turns around, one sock is missing! Biscuit is running across the field with the blue sock in his mouth, wagging his tail. Birimo chases him around the haystack, and Biscuit thinks it's the best game ever. Finally, Grandma Rowan whistles, and Biscuit drops the sock at her feet. It's wet and a bit muddy. A tiny gray cloud appears over Birimo's head, and it rumbles. Puff floats over and asks, Birimo, how are you really feeling? Are you angry? Birimo thinks for a moment. Then he laughs. I'm a little annoyed, not angry. Say it with me. I'm a little annoyed, not angry. Great job! The little cloud shrinks. Puff explains that feelings can be small, medium or big, just like temperatures. Let's read Puff's feelings thermometer card. "The Feelings Thermometer. From number one to number three, you are annoyed. At number one, you are just a little annoyed. Maybe your sock is wet, or someone keeps humming the same song. At number three, you are really annoyed, and maybe a bit grumpy. At number five, you are angry. Your face feels hot, and you want to stomp your feet. At the very top, at number seven, you are furious. That is the biggest, hottest kind of angry. All of these feelings are OK. But when you know your number, you can tell people clearly how you feel. And if your number is high, try this. Stop, take three slow breaths, and count to ten." What number is a little annoyed? Number one. What can you do when your number is high? Stop, take three slow breaths, and count to ten. Haru asks Birimo, How annoyed are you now? Birimo says, About a one. Maybe a zero, because Biscuit looks so sorry! Biscuit licks his hand, and the gray cloud disappears. Now, phonics. Jealous has e, a, but it sounds like a short e, and it ends in o, u, s. Confused has only one f. Grateful sounds like great, but we spell it g, r, a, t, e, plus f, u, l, with one l. Next time, Riko will have a muddy surprise in the village.

lessons.teacherScript: Hello, everyone! Last time, we said, I'm a little annoyed, not angry. Today, I take everyone down the hill to the village of Heatherbrook. The village green is busy. Some village children are playing ball near the old well. They wave at us, and Riko waves back with a big smile. But the path is wet after last night's rain. Riko steps on a slippery patch, her feet slide out, and splat! She sits down right in a puddle of mud. Riko starts to blush, and a soft pink mist appears all around her. She feels embarrassed（はずかしい）. Then a girl from the village giggles, and a boy calls out, Don't worry! That puddle catches everybody! I fell in it last week! The children laugh, but it's a kind laugh, and Riko starts laughing too. The girl helps her up and lends her a towel. The pink mist floats away, and the sun comes out. Later, Puff asks Riko how she really felt. Riko says, I was so embarrassed, but then I felt relieved. Say it with me. I was so embarrassed, but then I felt relieved. Wonderful! That evening, Riko writes in her diary. Let's read it. "Dear Diary, today I fell into a muddy puddle in front of all the village kids. At first, I wanted to hide under a rock. My face was hot, and a pink mist was all around me. Then a boy told me that the puddle catches everybody, and everyone laughed together. They weren't laughing at me. They were laughing with me. A girl helped me up, and she even lent me her towel. I felt so relieved! My heart went from stormy to sunny in one minute. Now I have some new friends in Heatherbrook, and I learned something important. Everybody makes mistakes, and a kind laugh can turn an embarrassing moment into a happy memory." What did the boy say about the puddle? It catches everybody. How did Riko feel at the end? Relieved. Puff turns a happy gold. Now, phonics. Furious ends with i, o, u, s. Lonely is lone plus l, y, so keep the e in the middle. Exhausted has a silent h after the x. After playing in the village all afternoon, Haru flops down on the grass and says, I'm exhausted! Next time, each of us will give a feelings weather report.

lessons.teacherScript: Hello, everyone! Last time, we said, I was so embarrassed, but then I felt relieved. Today, Grandma Rowan has an idea. Every evening, she listens to the weather report on her old radio. Why don't you make your own weather report, she says, a feelings weather report? Puff is so excited that the little cloud turns bright gold. We sit by the fire, and one by one, we stand up like real weather reporters. Kiko goes first. She's a little anxious about the village welcome party next week, but she's grateful for her new friends. So she says, Today, my feelings are cloudy with some sunshine. Say it with me. Today, my feelings are cloudy with some sunshine. Excellent! Next, it's Haru's turn. Let's read his weather report. "Good evening, everyone! Here is Haru's feelings weather report. This morning started bright and sunny, because we had Grandma Rowan's pancakes for breakfast. Around noon, there was a short shower of rain. I couldn't find my hat, and I was a bit frustrated. Luckily, Riko found it under the bench, so the rain stopped quickly. In the afternoon, there were strong winds of excitement, because we explored the stone walls and counted forty sheep. Tonight, I'm feeling warm and calm, with a light breeze of sleepiness. Tomorrow's forecast: sunny skies and lots of laughter, with a small chance of more pancakes. That's all from me. Back to you, Puff!" Why was Haru frustrated around noon? He couldn't find his hat. What's the forecast for tomorrow? Sunny skies and lots of laughter. Then Birimo gives his report. Tonight, it's sunny and sticky, with a one hundred percent chance of syrup! We laugh so hard that warm sunshine fills the room, even though it's night outside. Suddenly, Puff zooms to the window. Look at Heart Hill! A soft red light is glowing in the Great Rainbow. The red stripe came back! We learned to name our feelings, and red returned to the rainbow. Grandma Rowan wipes away a happy tear, and Biscuit wags his tail. Now, phonics. Let's review. Embarrassed has a double r and a double s. Anxious means a little worried, and it's spelled with an x and i, o, u, s. Grateful is grate plus f, u, l. Next time, Kiko will tell us about a problem with her flute.

lessons.teacherScript: Hello, everyone! Last time, we said, Today, my feelings are cloudy with some sunshine. Next Saturday, Heatherbrook will have a welcome party for us on the village green, and Kiko has been asked to play a highland tune on her flute. She practices every afternoon behind Grandma Rowan's farmhouse. But today, the high notes keep squeaking. Squeak! Squeak! Kiko stops, puts her flute in her lap and stares at her shoes. A little gray rain cloud appears right above her. Riko sits down next to her and holds an umbrella over her. She asks, What's wrong? Kiko says, My flute keeps squeaking. I've practiced so much, and it's still not right. Riko doesn't laugh, and she doesn't give advice. She just says softly, That must be hard. I'm sorry to hear that. Say it with me. That must be hard. I'm sorry to hear that. Very kind! Puff floats close and turns a gentle gray, too. Then Puff opens the Feelings Book to the advice corner. Let's read it. "Dear Puff, I have a problem. I'm learning to ride a bike, but I keep falling off. My big sister rides so easily. I feel sad, and I want to give up. From, Wobbly Wheels. Dear Wobbly Wheels, thank you for telling me how you feel. That must be hard. Learning something new can be really frustrating, especially when other people make it look easy. Remember, your sister was a beginner once, too. Every wobble means you are trying. Try practicing for ten minutes a day on soft grass. And if something ever feels really hard for a long time, talk to a grown-up you trust, like someone in your family or a teacher. Your friend, Puff." What is Wobbly Wheels learning to do? Ride a bike. Who can you talk to when something feels really hard for a long time? A grown-up you trust, like a family member or a teacher. Kiko smiles a tiny smile, and the rain cloud gets a little smaller. Now, phonics. These are phrasal verbs, two small words that work together. Cheer up means feel happier. Link the sounds, and cheer up sounds like chee-rup. Calm down means become quiet and peaceful again. Make up means become friends again after a fight. Say the second word strongly: cheer UP, calm DOWN, make UP. Next time, Haru will tell Kiko a story about his piano.

lessons.teacherScript: Hello, everyone! Last time, we said, That must be hard. I'm sorry to hear that. The next morning, Kiko is practicing again, but she still looks worried. The little rain cloud is back, following her like a balloon. Haru sits down beside her on the stone wall. He tells her that when he was little, he played the piano at his first recital. He practiced for weeks, but on the big day, his hands were shaking so much that he played the wrong notes. He wanted to run off the stage. He says, I know how you feel. I had the same problem. Say it with me. I know how you feel. I had the same problem. Wonderful! Kiko looks up. Really? You, Haru? Haru nods and shows her a page he wrote in Puff's Feelings Book last night. Let's read it. "My First Piano Recital, by Haru. The hall was big and bright, and every seat was full. When my name was called, my legs felt like jelly. I sat down at the piano, and my hands were shaking. In the middle of my song, I played three wrong notes in a row. My face got hot, and I wanted to disappear. But I took a deep breath and kept playing until the end. When I stood up to bow, my teacher was smiling, and my family was clapping loudly. After that, I practiced slowly, a little every day. At my next recital, I still made one small mistake, but I enjoyed the music. I learned that being nervous is normal, and that one mistake doesn't stop the music." What happened in the middle of Haru's song? He played three wrong notes in a row. What did Haru learn? Being nervous is normal, and one mistake doesn't stop the music. Kiko laughs a little. I had no idea you got nervous, too! Her rain cloud stops raining. Haru grins. Everybody gets nervous sometimes. Now, phonics. More phrasal verbs. Look up to means admire someone. Haru looks up to his piano teacher. Let down means disappoint. Kiko is afraid she will let everyone down. Get over means feel better after something sad or hard. Link the sounds in look up and get over, and say the little words strongly. Next time, Birimo has a problem with knitting, and Riko learns a new way to help.

lessons.teacherScript: Hello, everyone! Last time, we said, I know how you feel. I had the same problem. Kiko is practicing with a smile now. But today, someone else has a cloud over his head. It's Birimo! Grandma Rowan is teaching him to knit, because he wants to make a scarf for Puff. The problem is that his knitting keeps coming apart. The yarn gets tangled, the stitches slide off the needles, and his scarf has more holes than scarf. Birimo groans. A small cloud starts to rumble above him. Riko wants to help. But first, she asks a question. Do you want advice, or do you just want me to listen? Say it with me. Do you want advice, or do you just want me to listen? Great! Birimo thinks for a second and says, I just want you to listen, please. Riko listens and nods. After a few minutes, Birimo sighs. Thanks. I feel better. Now I'd like some advice! Let's read Puff's Feelings Book. "Two Ways to Help a Friend. When a friend is upset, we often want to fix the problem right away. We give advice, like Try this, or Don't worry. Sometimes that helps a lot. But sometimes a friend doesn't want ideas yet. They just want someone to hear how they feel. So before you help, ask, Do you want advice, or do you just want me to listen? If your friend wants you to listen, look at them, nod and let them finish. If they want advice, share one or two ideas kindly. And remember, if a problem feels too big for friends, it's a good idea to talk to a grown-up you trust, like a family member or a teacher." What should you ask before you help? Do you want advice, or do you just want me to listen? What can you do when a friend wants you to listen? Look at them, nod and let them finish. Grandma Rowan smiles and shows Birimo how to hold the needles. Slowly, the scarf begins to grow. Now, phonics. Open up means start to talk about your feelings. Birimo opened up to Riko. Count on means trust someone to help you. Stand up for means support someone when they need it. Link open up and count on. Say UP strongly in open up, but COUNT strongly in count on. Next time, it's the welcome party, and Kiko will play her flute!

lessons.teacherScript: Hello, everyone! Last time, we said, Do you want advice, or do you just want me to listen? Today is the day of the welcome party! Kiko has one last practice on the village green. She plays the highland tune from start to finish, but on the very last note, squeak! Her shoulders drop, and a tiny gray cloud starts to form. Haru jumps up. Cheer up! You'll do better next time. Say it with me. Cheer up! You'll do better next time. Super! Riko adds, You can do it! We're right here. Birimo does a silly dance to make her laugh, and it works. Before the party, each of us writes a cheer-up card to encourage Kiko. Let's read the cards. "Cheer-Up Cards for Kiko. From Haru: Cheer up! You'll do better next time. Remember my piano recital? One mistake doesn't stop the music. From Riko: You can do it! When you feel nervous, just look at us. We'll be smiling at you. From Birimo: If you squeak, I'll squeak too, and then it's a duet! From Ms. Emma: I'm so proud of how hard you've practiced. Breathe slowly and enjoy the tune. From Grandma Rowan: When I was a girl, I was shy, too. The hills don't care about perfect notes. They just want to hear your heart. From Puff: How are you really feeling? Whatever you feel, we're with you." What will Birimo do if Kiko squeaks? He'll squeak too, and then it's a duet. What do the hills want to hear, according to Grandma Rowan? Kiko's heart. That evening, the whole village gathers on the green. There are lanterns in the trees and a small wooden stage. Kiko steps onto the stage, holds her flute and looks at her friends. Then she plays. There's one tiny squeak in the middle, but she keeps going, and the tune flies over the hills. The villagers start clapping and dancing, and the setting sun glows warm and golden. Kiko's face is full of confidence. Riko asks, How did it go? Kiko beams. It went really well! Now, phonics. Put up with means accept something annoying. Grandma Rowan puts up with Biscuit's sock stealing. Work out means end well. Everything worked out for Kiko. Turn to means go to someone for help. Kiko can turn to her friends. Next time, we'll practice being good listeners.

lessons.teacherScript: Hello, everyone! Last time, we said, Cheer up! You'll do better next time. The morning after the party, I have a plan. I say, You've learned so much about listening. Let's practice being good listeners with a role-play. One person tells a small problem, and the other person listens. Riko and Kiko go first. Riko pretends that her painting of the purple heather got muddy, because Biscuit walked right across it. Kiko looks at her kindly, nods and says, Tell me what happened. Say it with me. Tell me what happened. Perfect! Grandma Rowan pins a poster on the kitchen wall. Let's read it. "How to Be a Good Listener. Step one: Stop what you are doing, and look at your friend kindly. Step two: Invite them to talk. You can say, Tell me what happened. Step three: Listen to the whole story. Nod, and don't interrupt, even if you have a great idea. Step four: Ask gentle questions, like Then what happened? or How do you feel now? Step five: Show that you understand. Say, That must be hard, or I know how you feel. Step six: Ask, Do you want advice, or do you just want me to listen? Good listeners don't have to fix everything. Sometimes a friend just needs a warm, quiet place to calm down. And if a problem is very big, help your friend find a grown-up they can count on." What can you say to invite a friend to talk? Tell me what happened. What should you do even if you have a great idea? Don't interrupt. Riko tells the whole story, and Kiko listens without interrupting once. At the end, Kiko asks, How do you feel now? Riko says, I feel calmer. Thanks for listening. I remind everyone that if something is really hard, we can always talk to a grown-up we trust, like a family member or a teacher. Suddenly, the kitchen glows. Puff zooms to the window. Look! A warm orange light is spreading across the Great Rainbow. Orange returned to the rainbow! We learned to listen with our hearts. Now, phonics. Let's review. Calm down means become peaceful again. Count on means trust someone to help you. Relieved has i before e. Next time, we'll walk toward Heart Hill with a map, but Haru and Riko won't agree about the way.

lessons.teacherScript: Hello, everyone! Last time, we said, Tell me what happened. Today, we set off for the spring at the top of Heart Hill with a map from Grandma Rowan. Above the hill, the Great Rainbow shows its red and orange stripes. Soon we reach a fork in the path. Haru grabs the map and says, Let's go left. It's shorter! Riko frowns and says, But Grandma Rowan said the right path is better. Haru insists, Left! I've got the map! Riko raises her voice. You never listen! Haru raises his voice, too. Then thick gray fog rolls in around us. Puff turns gray and whispers, Oh dear. Haru and Riko had a fight about the map. Say it with me. Haru and Riko had a fight about the map. Good. I calmly say, Everyone, stop here and stay close to me. We'll wait until the fog thins. We're all together, and nobody is lost. Let's read a page from Puff's Feelings Book. "Puff's Feelings Book, Page Twelve: When Friends Argue. Even the best of friends argue sometimes. That's normal, and it doesn't mean the friendship is over. An argument often starts with something small, like a map, a game or the last cookie. Then the feelings get bigger. One friend feels ignored. The other friend feels that nobody trusts them. Voices get louder, and nobody is really listening anymore. In the Highlands, this is when the fog rolls in. The fog here makes everything hard to see, just like anger does. When the fog comes, stop walking. Stand still, take a slow breath and wait. Little by little, the fog will thin, and you will see your friend again. Remember, fog never lasts forever." What often starts an argument? Something small, like a map, a game or the last cookie. What should you do when the fog comes? Stop walking, stand still and take a slow breath. So we wait. Haru and Riko stand apart without a word. Now, phonics. The same words can sound kind or unkind, depending on your voice. When a friend has sad news, use a low, soft voice that falls. Oh no. When a friend has good news, use a high, bright voice that goes up and down. That's great! When you're surprised or checking, let your voice go up. Really? Next time, someone will find the words to say sorry.

lessons.teacherScript: Hello, everyone! Last time, we said, Haru and Riko had a fight about the map. Today, we are still waiting in the fog. We sit close together on a big flat rock beside the path. Nobody is in danger, but nobody is talking, either. Puff floats down next to Haru and asks softly, How are you really feeling? Haru sighs. I feel bad. I grabbed the map, and I didn't let Riko speak. Puff says, Then maybe you can tell her that. Haru walks over to Riko and says, Riko, I'm sorry. I didn't mean to hurt you. Say it with me. I'm sorry. I didn't mean to hurt you. Well done! Riko looks up. I'm sorry too, she says quietly. I didn't mean to shout at you. Let's read a letter from Puff's advice corner. "Ask Puff. Dear Puff, Yesterday, I knocked over my friend's tower of blocks by accident. She cried, and I felt terrible. I said sorry, but then I said it was only a pile of blocks. Now she won't play with me. What should I do? From, Oops in the Hills. Dear Oops, Thank you for writing to me. It's clear that you care about your friend. A good apology has three parts. First, say what happened: I knocked over your tower. Second, say sorry and show that you understand: I didn't mean to, but I know you worked hard on it. Third, offer to help: Can I help you build it again? Try not to say it was only a small thing. Then give your friend a little time. Love, Puff." What did Oops in the Hills do by accident? Oops knocked over a friend's tower of blocks. What are the three parts of a good apology? Say what happened, say sorry, and offer to help. The fog is a little thinner now. Haru and Riko are sitting side by side, although they are still a bit quiet. That's OK. Making up can take time. Now, phonics. When a friend tells you something sad, speak low and soft, and let your voice fall. That must be hard. When a friend has great news, use a bright voice that goes up and then down. Congratulations! When you're worried about someone, let your voice go up at the end. Are you OK? Next time, Haru and Riko will think about what they could do differently.

lessons.teacherScript: Hello, everyone! Last time, we said, I'm sorry. I didn't mean to hurt you. Today, the fog is thinner, but it hasn't gone away. We can see a stone wall and a few sheep again, although Heart Hill is still hidden. I say, Saying sorry was a great first step. Now let's think back. What happened, and what can we do differently next time? Puff pulls a small card out of the mist. It's a Think-Back Card. Haru reads the first question and thinks hard. Then he turns to Riko and says, I should have listened to you. Say it with me. I should have listened to you. Excellent! Riko smiles a little. And I could have explained it more calmly, she says. Let's read the Think-Back Card that Haru and Riko filled out together. "Puff's Think-Back Card. Question one: What happened? Haru: I grabbed the map and said we had to go left. Riko: I wanted to go right, and I shouted. Question two: How did you feel? Haru: At first, I felt proud of my plan. Then I felt bad. Riko: I felt ignored and frustrated. Question three: What should you have done? Haru: I should have listened to Riko. I should have asked everyone what they thought. Riko: I could have told Haru my reason before I got upset. Question four: What will you do next time? Haru: I'll share the map. Riko: I'll take a deep breath before I speak. Puff's note: Thinking back is not about feeling bad. It's about learning, so that the next walk is a happier one." How did Riko feel? Ignored and frustrated. What will Haru do next time? Share the map. As they finish the card, a soft breeze blows, and the fog drifts away a little more. Puff changes from gray to a light silver. Now, phonics. Let's practice our kind voices again. When something sad happens, say it softly and let your voice fall. I'm so sorry. When a friend does something good, sound bright and go up, then down. Good for you! When you want to check on someone, go up at the end. Is everything all right? Next time, will the fog finally clear?

lessons.teacherScript: Hello, everyone! Last time, we said, I should have listened to you. Today, Haru and Riko stand up from the rock. Haru holds out the map. Let's read it together this time, he says. Then he holds out his other hand. Riko, let's make up. Friends? Say it with me. Let's make up. Friends? Great! Riko grins and shakes his hand. Friends! At that moment, something wonderful happens. The fog begins to lift, like a curtain opening on a stage. First we see the stone walls, then the purple heather, and then the top of Heart Hill, shining in the sun. Warm sunbeams fall on our faces, and Puff turns bright gold. Together, we take the right path, and soon we reach the spring. The water is clear and cold, and it sparkles like glass. Beside it, there is a little wooden box with a letter inside. Let's read it. "Dear friends, If you are reading this, you have reached the Spring of Heart Hill. Well done! Many people who come here have had a hard walk. Some got tired. Some got lost. Some had an argument on the way. When I was young, I argued with my best friend on this very path, and we didn't speak for a whole morning. Then we sat down here, drank this cold water and started to laugh. Making up is like this spring. It's simple, but it makes you feel fresh again. You don't need perfect words. Say sorry, say what you will do next time, and then do something together. Drink some water, look at the view and enjoy your friendship. With love, Grandma Rowan." What happened when Grandma Rowan argued with her best friend? They didn't speak for a whole morning. What does she say making up is like? This spring. Haru and Riko scoop up the water and drink it at the same time. Then Birimo slips on a wet stone and sits down with a splash! I ask, Did it hurt? Just a little, he says, but now his bottom is wet. Everyone laughs. Now, phonics. Let's listen to three more kind voices. Kiko's sandwich fell in the stream. That's too bad. Low and falling. The sun came out! How wonderful! Bright, up and down. Birimo slipped on the stones. Did it hurt? Up at the end. Next time, we'll share what we learned with the children of Heatherbrook.

lessons.teacherScript: Hello, everyone! Last time, we said, Let's make up. Friends? Today, we are back in Heatherbrook, and Grandma Rowan has a request. The children at the little village school sometimes argue, too, she says. Could you make a poster to help them? So, at Grandma Rowan's big kitchen table, we get to work. Haru draws the pictures, Riko writes the words, Kiko adds the colors, and Birimo adds lots of tiny hearts. Then we carry the poster to the village school, where twelve children are waiting. Haru and Riko stand in front of them together. Riko points to the poster and reads the four steps. Calm down. Listen. Say how you feel. Find a solution. Say it with me. Calm down. Listen. Say how you feel. Find a solution. Fantastic! Let's read the poster. "Four Steps to Solve a Fight. Step one: Calm down. When you feel angry, stop. Take three deep breaths, or count to ten. Big feelings are OK, but it's hard to think clearly when you're upset. Step two: Listen. Let the other person speak, and don't interrupt. Try to understand their reason. Step three: Say how you feel. Use I sentences, like I felt sad when you took the map. Never call people names. Step four: Find a solution. Think of an idea that works for both of you. You could take turns, share, or choose together. Then shake hands and make up. Remember, everyone argues sometimes. What matters is what you do next. Made by Haru, Riko, Kiko and Birimo, with help from Puff." What can you do in step one? Take three deep breaths, or count to ten. What should you do in step two? Let the other person speak, and don't interrupt. The children clap, and a small boy raises his hand. I had a fight with my sister yesterday, he says. That must be hard, says Kiko gently. But we made up this morning, he adds. We all cheer, That's great! At that moment, warm sunshine pours through the window. Look! The yellow stripe came back to the Great Rainbow! Now it has red, orange and yellow. Now, phonics. Let's review. That must be hard, low and soft. That's great! Bright and happy. Make up, link the words and say up strongly. Lonely is lone plus l, y, so keep the e. Next time, Riko has a plan that starts very early in the morning.

lessons.teacherScript: Hello, everyone! Last time, we said, Calm down. Listen. Say how you feel. Find a solution. Today, we are having dinner at Grandma Rowan's farmhouse. The rainbow above Heart Hill now has three colors, and Puff says the next color needs a new heart skill. Grandma Rowan tells us that the sunrise from the top of Heart Hill is the most beautiful sight in the highlands. Riko's eyes light up. But Haru yawns and says, I want to sleep late tomorrow. And I want pancakes for breakfast, says Birimo. Riko thinks for a moment. Then she says, Wouldn't it be better if we left early? We could see the sunrise, the air is cool in the morning, and we can take the pancakes with us for a picnic on the hilltop! Say it with me. Wouldn't it be better if we left early? Very good! Riko gives reasons, and she thinks about what everyone wants. Let's read a page from Puff's Feelings Book. "Puff's Feelings Book, Page Twenty: How to Persuade Kindly. Sometimes you want your friends to agree with your idea. That's fine! But persuading is not the same as bossing people around. Here are some tips. First, think about what the other person wants. Second, give clear reasons, and explain how your idea helps everyone, not only you. Third, use gentle questions, like Wouldn't it be better if we tried this? or How about this? Fourth, listen to their worries and answer them. Maybe your friend is tired, or hungry, or a little scared. Finally, remember that your friend can say no. A good persuader smiles, respects the answer and stays a good friend. If they say yes, wonderful! If they say no, that's OK too." What is the first tip? Think about what the other person wants. What should you remember at the end? Your friend can say no. Haru thinks about it. Cool air, a sunrise and pancakes on the hilltop? OK, you've persuaded me! Birimo is over the moon. I set my alarm clock for four o'clock. Now, phonics. Today, we learn idioms about feelings. When you are very, very happy, you're over the moon. When you feel sad, you feel blue. When something is very easy, it's a piece of cake. But getting up at four o'clock is not a piece of cake! Next time, at dawn, Birimo has an idea of his own.

lessons.teacherScript: Hello, everyone! Last time, we said, Wouldn't it be better if we left early? Today, it's half past four in the morning. The stars are still out. We walk quietly out of the farmhouse with our flashlights. Puff glows softly beside us like a little lamp. At the foot of Heart Hill, there are two paths. The short path goes straight up. The long path curves along a high ridge. Birimo stops and says, Let's take the long path! Haru frowns and says, But it's longer, and we might miss the sunrise. Birimo says, Grandma Rowan told me a secret. From the ridge, you can see a sea of clouds at dawn. Trust me. It'll be worth it. Say it with me. Trust me. It'll be worth it. Wonderful! I check my watch. We have time. Let's read the note Grandma Rowan wrote on the back of our map. "The Ridge Path. This path is about twenty minutes longer than the short path, but it is my favorite walk in the whole highlands. It is wide and safe, with a stone wall on one side, so just walk steadily and stay together. On cool, still mornings, the valleys below fill with white mist. When the sun comes up, the mist turns pink and gold, and it looks like a soft, shining sea. The hills poke out of it like little islands. I call it the sea of clouds. Not many people see it, because most people take the shortcut or stay in bed! If you reach the big flat rock before sunrise, sit down, eat something warm and wait. You won't be sorry. Grandma Rowan." How much longer is the ridge path? About twenty minutes. Why don't many people see the sea of clouds? Because most people take the shortcut or stay in bed. We reach the big flat rock just in time. Below us, the valleys are full of white clouds. Then the sun rises, and the whole sea turns pink and gold. Haru whispers, Birimo, you were right. It was worth it. Now, phonics. More idioms! When you are nervous, you have butterflies in your stomach. When you are super happy, you're on cloud nine. When you say the first friendly words to someone new, you break the ice. Next time, back in the village, we'll meet someone who needs a friend.

lessons.teacherScript: Hello, everyone! Last time, we said, Trust me. It'll be worth it. Today, we're back in Heatherbrook. On the village green, children are playing tag. But at the edge of the green, a boy named Finn is sitting on his own. He watches the game, but he doesn't join in, and a tiny gray cloud floats above his head. Kiko says, I think he wants to play, but he's too shy to ask. Riko has an idea. She says, At my school, we have a buddy bench. When you sit on it, it means you'd like someone to play with, and other kids come and invite you. We go to see Mr. Bram, the village leader. He has a big gray beard. He listens, strokes his beard and says, Hmm. A bench takes money and work. Haru answers, If we do this, everyone will benefit. Say it with me. If we do this, everyone will benefit. Super! Let's read the idea sheet we wrote for Mr. Bram. "Our Idea: A Buddy Bench for Heatherbrook. What is it? A buddy bench is a bench where you sit when you want someone to play with. When other children see someone on the bench, they go over and say, Do you want to play with us? Why do we need it? Some children feel shy, and it's hard for them to ask to join a game. New children and visitors often don't know anyone. A buddy bench makes it easy to find a friend. Who will benefit? Shy children, new children, visitors and everyone who wants more friends. How can we do it? There is old wood in the village barn. We will help paint the bench, and we will show the children how it works. Thank you for reading!" Who will benefit? Shy children, new children, visitors and everyone who wants more friends. Where is the wood? In the village barn. Mr. Bram reads it, smiles and says, It's a fine idea, but the village decides together. Come to the village hall in two days and tell everyone. Haru gulps. A speech? Riko says, Keep your chin up. We'll do it together. Now, phonics. If you feel a little sick, you're under the weather. To tell someone to stay brave, say keep your chin up. If you suddenly feel too nervous to do something, you get cold feet. Next time, we'll get some surprising invitations.

lessons.teacherScript: Hello, everyone! Last time, we said, If we do this, everyone will benefit. Today, we are getting ready for our speeches at the village hall. But first, we get some surprising invitations. On the way to the village green, we meet Finn and his big brother, Rory. Rory has a towel around his neck. Dad is taking us for a quick swim in the lake, he says. Want to come? Haru looks at the lake. It is blue, beautiful and freezing cold. Haru smiles and says, Thanks for asking, but I'd rather not. Say it with me. Thanks for asking, but I'd rather not. Nice! Rory just laughs. No problem! Then Finn says very quietly, I don't like cold water, either. It's the first time he has spoken to us! Later, Grandma Rowan offers us her famous gooseberry juice. It is super sour. Birimo takes one sip, and his face goes small and wrinkly. Let's read a page from Puff's Feelings Book. "Puff's Feelings Book, Page Twenty-Three: Saying No Politely. Sometimes people invite you to do something, and you don't want to. Maybe it doesn't feel safe, maybe you don't like it, or maybe you're just tired. It's OK to say no. You can say no and still be kind. Try these three steps. First, say thank you: Thanks for asking. Second, say no clearly: but I'd rather not, or no, thank you. Third, if you like, give a short reason or suggest something else: Maybe we can play cards later. You don't have to give a long excuse. And when someone says no to you, remember that it's not about you. Just smile and say, That's OK. A kind no and a kind answer keep a friendship strong." What is the first step? Say thank you. What can you say when someone says no to you? That's OK. Grandma Rowan offers Birimo a second glass. Birimo smiles and says, Thanks for asking, but I'd rather not. Could I have some water instead? Grandma Rowan laughs so hard that her woolly hat falls off. She doesn't lose her temper at all. She has a heart of gold. Now, phonics. When you listen very carefully, you're all ears. When someone is very kind, they have a heart of gold. When you suddenly get very angry, you lose your temper. Tomorrow is the big day at the village hall. Are you ready?

lessons.teacherScript: Hello, everyone! Last time, we said, Thanks for asking, but I'd rather not. Today is the Persuasion Challenge at the village hall. The hall is full of villagers sitting on long wooden benches. Grandma Rowan is in the front row with Biscuit at her feet, and Finn is sitting next to his brother. Mr. Bram stands at the front. Haru's hands are shaking. Kiko asks, Are you OK? Haru nods. I'm nervous, but I'm ready. One by one, we speak. Kiko talks about new children. Haru talks about visitors. Birimo makes everyone laugh with a funny drawing. Then Riko steps forward and begins, Let me tell you why this is a great idea. Say it with me. Let me tell you why this is a great idea. Great job! Let's read Riko's speech. "Good evening, everyone. Let me tell you why this is a great idea. Imagine you are new in a village. You see children playing, and you want to join them, but you feel too shy to ask. Maybe you feel frustrated, or a little lonely. A buddy bench can help. When you sit on it, everyone knows that you want someone to play with. Then a kind child comes over and says, Come and play with us! First, it helps shy children and new children. Second, it teaches all of us to notice each other. Third, it's easy. There is wood in the barn, and we will help paint the bench. Heatherbrook is a warm village. With a buddy bench, it can be even warmer. Thank you for listening." What are Riko's three reasons? It helps shy and new children, it teaches us to notice each other, and it's easy. Where is the wood? In the barn. Then Mr. Bram asks the villagers to vote. Hands go up everywhere. Mr. Bram smiles under his big gray beard and says, The answer is yes! The village carpenter offers to build the bench next week. Finn's little gray cloud melts away, and he smiles. At that moment, sunlight fills the windows. Look! The green stripe came back to the Great Rainbow! Now there are four colors: red, orange, yellow and green. Now, phonics. Let's review. Over the moon means very happy. Are you OK? Let your voice go up. Cheer up, link the words and say up strongly. Frustrated has no extra e. Next time, we'll talk about people we look up to.

lessons.teacherScript: Hello, everyone! Last time, we said, Let me tell you why this is a great idea. Mr. Bram said yes, and next week the buddy bench will be built on the village green! This morning, we are sitting around the big wooden table in Grandma Rowan's farmhouse kitchen. Biscuit is asleep under Birimo's chair, and Puff floats above the teapot, glowing a soft gold. Grandma Rowan pours warm milk and asks a big question. Who do you look up to? To look up to someone means to admire them and want to be a little like them. Haru looks up to his swimming coach, because she is always kind, even when he is slow. Kiko looks up to her grandpa, who can fix almost anything. Birimo shouts, I look up to Puff! Puff turns pink. Then Riko smiles and says, I look up to my aunt because she's so patient. Say it with me. I look up to my aunt because she's so patient. Great! Let's read the page Riko wrote in her notebook. "Someone I Look Up To. I look up to my aunt because she's so patient. Last summer, she taught me how to ride a bike. I fell over again and again, and I wanted to give up. My aunt never got annoyed. She just said, Let's try one more time, and she held the back of my seat. When I finally rode to the end of our street, she cheered louder than anyone. My aunt is also very helpful. When our neighbor's garden was full of weeds, she spent a whole Saturday pulling them out with him. She never makes a big fuss about it. She just helps. I want to be like her when I grow up, because she makes people feel that they can do it." What did Riko's aunt teach her? How to ride a bike. What did her aunt say when Riko fell over? Let's try one more time. A role model can be someone close to you, says Grandma Rowan. Now, phonics. Many character words end in -ful, -ive or -ous. Helpful is help plus -ful, which means full of help. Creative ends in -ive and means good at making new things. Generous ends in -ous and means happy to give and share. Kiko's grandpa is helpful, creative and generous! Next time, we'll learn how to ask deep interview questions.

lessons.teacherScript: Hello, everyone! Last time, we said, I look up to my aunt because she's so patient. This morning, Mr. Bram knocks on the farmhouse door with exciting news. On Saturday, the village hall will hold an Interview Show, and he wants us to be the interviewers! Our guest will be a very special person, but he won't tell us who yet. He just winks and strokes his big gray beard. I say, A good interview is like a good conversation. Don't just ask yes-or-no questions. Ask questions that open doors. I write three questions on the board. Why? How did you feel at that moment? What did you learn? Haru practices by interviewing Kiko about the welcome party, when she played her flute again. He asks, What happened? Kiko says, My hands were shaking before I started. Then Haru asks the deep question. How did you feel at that moment? Say it with me. How did you feel at that moment? Excellent! Let's read Puff's interview tips card. "Puff's Five Interview Tips. One: Start with an easy question to help your guest relax. Two: Ask open questions that start with why, how or what. A yes-or-no question gives you one word, but an open question gives you a story. Three: Ask about feelings. How did you feel at that moment? What was it like? Four: Listen carefully, and ask a follow-up question. If your guest says, I was nervous, you can ask, What helped you feel better? Five: Near the end, ask, What did you learn? Remember, an interview is not a test. Be thoughtful and kind. If your guest doesn't want to answer a question, that's OK. Just say, No problem, and move on. And always say thank you at the end!" What kind of question gives you a story? An open question. What can you say if your guest doesn't want to answer? No problem. Kiko answers Haru with a big smile. At first I was scared, but then I felt really proud. Puff glows gold. Now, phonics. Thoughtful ends in -ful. It means full of thought, so a thoughtful person thinks about others. Sensitive ends in -ive. A sensitive person notices other people's feelings. Courageous ends in -ous. Keep the e in courage, then add -ous! It means very brave. Next time, we'll find out who our special guest is.

lessons.teacherScript: Hello, everyone! Last time, we said, How did you feel at that moment? Today, Mr. Bram finally tells us the name of our guest for the Interview Show. It's Grandma Rowan! She laughs and says, Oh my, I'm not famous! But Mr. Bram says that everyone in Heatherbrook has a story about her. So this evening, we sit by the fire in her farmhouse and do a practice interview. Biscuit rests his head on her knee. Kiko holds the notebook, Haru holds a pretend microphone, and I sit with them, ready to help. Riko asks the first question. Grandma Rowan, what was your childhood like? Say it with me. What was your childhood like? Wonderful! Let's read Kiko's interview notes. "Interview Notes: Grandma Rowan. Childhood: She grew up on a farm in these highlands, with sheep, chickens and an old pony. She was a cheerful, adventurous girl who loved climbing stone walls. Dream: She wanted to be an animal doctor, because she loved caring for sick lambs. Problem: The nearest school was far away, over three hills. She walked there every day, in sunshine, wind and rain. Hard moment: She failed an important exam once. She felt terrible and cried behind the barn. What helped: Her teacher was very supportive. She said, One exam doesn't decide who you are. Ending: She studied hard, tried again and passed. She became the animal doctor for the whole highlands! Now she is retired and keeps sheep." How far away was the school? Over three hills. What did her teacher say? One exam doesn't decide who you are. Then Haru asks a follow-up question. How did you feel when you failed the exam? Grandma Rowan looks into the fire for a moment. Very disappointed, she says. But I learned that falling down is part of climbing. Puff turns a soft gray, and then a warm gold again. Now, phonics. Cheerful ends in -ful. It means full of cheer, so a cheerful person smiles a lot. Supportive ends in -ive. A supportive person helps you keep going. Adventurous ends in -ous. An adventurous person loves exploring and trying new things. Young Rowan was cheerful and adventurous, and her teacher was supportive. Next time, we'll turn these notes into an interview article.

lessons.teacherScript: Hello, everyone! Last time, we said, What was your childhood like? Today, we're turning our interview into an article for the Heatherbrook Village News, a little newspaper that is pinned up outside the village shop every Friday. I explain how an article works. First, you need a headline that catches the reader's eye. Next, an opening that tells who, what and where. Then you share the most interesting parts of the story, with quotes. A quote is the exact words that someone said. In writing, we put those words inside quotation marks and say who said them. Riko reads her favorite quote from our notes. Grandma Rowan said, I never gave up. I write it on the board with quotation marks. 'I never gave up,' she told me. Say it with me. 'I never gave up,' she told me. Perfect! Let's read the article we wrote together. "From Lambs to Legends: Meet Grandma Rowan. Everyone in Heatherbrook knows Grandma Rowan, the kind shepherd in the woolly hat. But did you know she was once the animal doctor for the whole highlands? As a girl, she dreamed of caring for animals. Her school was three hills away, and she walked there every day. 'The wind tried to push me home, but I kept walking,' she laughed. When she failed an important exam, she wanted to quit. Her supportive teacher helped her try again. 'I never gave up,' she told me. Today she is retired, but she still looks after her sheep, with help from her playful sheepdog, Biscuit. Her advice for children? 'Be attentive to animals and people. They will tell you what they need.'" Where is the Village News pinned up? Outside the village shop. What is Grandma Rowan's advice? Be attentive to animals and people. Birimo wants to add a joke at the bottom of the page. He writes, Biscuit would like everyone to know that he is the real boss of the farm. We all laugh, and I say we can keep it. Now, phonics. Playful ends in -ful. It means full of play, like Biscuit chasing his tail. Attentive ends in -ive. An attentive person pays close attention. Humorous ends in -ous. A humorous person makes people laugh, just like Birimo! Next time, it's the big Interview Show at the village hall!

lessons.teacherScript: Hello, everyone! Last time, we said, 'I never gave up,' she told me. Tonight is the Interview Show! The village hall is full. Families sit on wooden benches, Finn waves from the front row, and Mr. Bram stands at the back with a big smile under his gray beard. On the stage, there are two armchairs, a little table with a vase of purple heather, and a microphone. Riko is the host. She steps up to the microphone, takes a deep breath and says, Good evening, everyone! Welcome to the Interview Show. Our guest today is Grandma Rowan. Say it with me. Our guest today is Grandma Rowan. Fantastic! Let's read the program for the show. "The Heatherbrook Interview Show. Tonight at seven, in the village hall. Host: Riko. Interviewers: Haru, Kiko and Birimo. Special guest: Grandma Rowan, shepherd and former animal doctor of the highlands. Part one: Growing up on the farm. Part two: The long walk to school. Part three: The exam that changed everything. Part four: Questions from the audience. Please raise your hand if you want to ask a question, and wait for the microphone. Biscuit the sheepdog will also be on stage. Please do not feed him, even if he looks at you with big, sad eyes. After the show, there will be warm scones and tea for everyone. Thank you for coming, and remember Puff's question: How are you really feeling?" Who is the host? Riko. What should you do if you want to ask a question? Raise your hand and wait for the microphone. The interview goes wonderfully. Haru asks about the long walk, Kiko asks about the exam, and Birimo asks if sheep ever feel blue. Of course they do, says Grandma Rowan, and they get over it with a good friend and fresh grass! Everyone laughs. Then a little girl in the audience asks, Were you ever scared? Many times, says Grandma Rowan, but I was never alone. My friends helped me. Through the window, we see Heart Hill. The blue stripe came back to the Great Rainbow! Now, phonics. Let's review. Generous ends in -ous, and thoughtful ends in -ful. Grandma Rowan is generous with her time and thoughtful with her words. To feel blue means to feel sad. To get over something means to feel better after something sad. Next time, we'll have a quiz about feeling idioms!

lessons.teacherScript: Hello, everyone! Last time, we said, Our guest today is Grandma Rowan. Today, a gentle rain is falling on Heatherbrook, so Grandma Rowan has a plan. She brings out a small brass bell and says, Welcome to the Heart Idiom Quiz! An idiom is a group of words with a special meaning. You can't guess it from each single word. For example, a piece of cake（とても かんたん）doesn't really mean cake. It means very easy. Birimo looks worried. No cake? Grandma Rowan laughs and puts a plate of real cake on the table, too. Haru rings the bell first and says, Over the moon means very, very happy! Correct! Kiko knows feel blue. It means feel sad. Riko knows butterflies in my stomach. It means feeling nervous. Kiko says she felt a little jealous when Haru rang the bell so fast, but then she rings it first for the next question! Then Birimo winks at me and asks, Learning English is a piece of cake now? I laugh. Not yet! But we're getting better every day. Say it with me. Learning English is a piece of cake now? Not yet! Ha! Great! Let's read the quiz card. "Heart Idiom Quiz. Question one: Mia's team won the final match. She is over the moon. How does Mia feel? Answer: very happy. Question two: Tom's best friend moved to another town, and Tom feels blue. How does Tom feel? Answer: sad. Question three: Before her dance show, Lily has butterflies in her stomach. How does Lily feel? Answer: nervous. Question four: The spelling test was a piece of cake for Ben. Was it hard for him? Answer: no, it was very easy. Bonus question: Which idiom means you suddenly feel too nervous to do something? Answer: get cold feet. Well done! Idioms make your English colorful, so try to use them at the right moment." How does Tom feel? Sad. What does a piece of cake mean? Very easy. Now, phonics. Let's review. In jealous, the e and a together sound like a short e. In look up to, link look and up, and say UP strongly. Oh no goes down, soft and slow. Butterflies in my stomach means nervous. Creative ends in -ive. Riko makes up a creative new saying. As warm as Grandma Rowan's kitchen! Next time, we'll write letters to people who are important to us.

lessons.teacherScript: Hello, everyone! Last time, we said, Learning English is a piece of cake now? Not yet! Today, Grandma Rowan gives each of us a sheet of creamy writing paper and an envelope with a tiny sprig of heather on it. In the highlands, she says, we write the most important things in letters, because a letter can be read again and again. Haru writes to his swimming coach. Riko writes to her aunt. Birimo writes to Puff, even though Puff is floating right next to him! Kiko is quiet. She wants to write to her best friend, who moved to another town last spring. A small gray cloud appears over Kiko's head. Puff floats close and asks, How are you really feeling? Kiko says, I miss her. But I want her to know she's still my friend. Then she writes, I wanted to tell you how much you mean to me. Say it with me. I wanted to tell you how much you mean to me. Beautiful! Let's read Kiko's letter. "Dear Sora, How are you? I'm writing from the Highlands of the Heart, where the weather changes with your feelings. It's sunny right now, because I'm thinking about you. I was disappointed when you moved away, and at first I didn't want to talk about it. But here, I learned to open up. So, I wanted to tell you how much you mean to me. You were always so supportive. When I was nervous before my recital, you held my hand. You have a heart of gold. I hope your new town is fun and you're making lots of friends. Please write back soon and tell me everything! I'm sending you a pressed heather flower. Your friend forever, Kiko" Where is Kiko writing from? The Highlands of the Heart. What did Sora do before Kiko's recital? She held Kiko's hand. When Kiko finishes, the gray cloud melts into sunshine. Haru says, Good for you, Kiko. That was brave. Tomorrow, we'll mail our letters together. Now, phonics. Let's review. Disappointed has one s and double p. In open up, link open and up, and say UP strongly. Good for you goes high and then down, bright and happy. A heart of gold means very kind. Supportive ends in -ive. Next time, we'll start a kindness chain in Heatherbrook!

lessons.teacherScript: Hello, everyone! Last time, we said, I wanted to tell you how much you mean to me. This morning, the buddy bench is finally ready! Mr. Bram painted it bright red, and it stands under the old oak tree on the village green. I have an idea. Let's start a kindness chain. Each person says one kind word or does one kind thing for someone, and then that person passes it on. Haru starts. He tells the baker, Your bread smells amazing! The baker smiles and gives a warm roll to a tired farmer. The farmer thanks the mail carrier for bringing letters in the rain. The mail carrier helps a girl named Ellie carry a heavy basket. Then Ellie sees Finn sitting on the buddy bench. She sits down next to him and asks, Do you want to play? Finn looks up. Really? You want to play with me? Soon they are laughing and running together. I say, One kind word can change someone's day. Say it with me. One kind word can change someone's day. Wonderful! Let's read the poster we made for the village shop. "Join the Heatherbrook Kindness Chain! How does it work? It's easy. Say one kind word or do one kind thing for someone. Then ask them to pass it on. Here are some ideas. Say thank you to someone who helps you. Tell a friend who feels down, Keep your chin up. Stand up for someone who is being left out. Smile at someone new. Help carry a heavy bag. Sit with someone on the buddy bench. Kindness doesn't have to be big. Even a cheerful hello can change someone's day. When you are kind, you feel happy too, and the sky over the highlands gets sunnier! How long can our chain be? Let's find out together!" What can you say to a friend who feels down? Keep your chin up. Where can you sit with someone? On the buddy bench. By sunset, the chain has forty-two kind words! Now, phonics. Let's review. Exhausted has a silent h after the x. In stand up for, link stand and up, and say UP strongly. Really with a rising voice shows you're surprised. Keep your chin up means stay brave. Cheerful ends in -ful. By the evening, we're exhausted but cheerful! Next time, we'll take a goodbye walk and look back on our adventure.

lessons.teacherScript: Hello, everyone! Last time, we said, One kind word can change someone's day. Today, we take a goodbye walk around the highlands with Puff, Grandma Rowan and Biscuit. We pass the muddy spot where Riko slipped, and she laughs. We pass the village hall where we gave our speeches, and the fork in the path where Haru and Riko had their fight. I'm glad we made up, says Haru. Me too, says Riko. But Birimo is very quiet, and a tiny rain cloud is following him. Puff floats over and asks, How are you really feeling? Birimo says, I'm going to miss Biscuit so much. I've felt sad all morning. Haru puts his arm around him and says, That must be hard for you. I should have noticed sooner. Say it with me. That must be hard for you. I should have noticed sooner. Well done! Let's read the last page of Puff's Feelings Book. "What We Learned in the Highlands of the Heart. First, we learned many feeling words. Now we can say that we are over the moon, a little annoyed, or embarrassed but relieved. Next, we learned to listen. We say, That must be hard, or Tell me what happened, and we don't interrupt. Then Haru and Riko had a fight. They learned to say, I didn't mean to hurt you, and I should have listened, and they made up. After that, we learned to persuade with kind reasons, and to say no politely. Finally, we interviewed Grandma Rowan and learned that asking good questions is a way of caring. Most of all, we learned that every feeling is OK, and sharing it helps." What do good listeners say? That must be hard, or Tell me what happened. What did we learn most of all? Every feeling is OK, and sharing it helps. Just then, Biscuit runs up and licks Birimo's nose. Birimo giggles. Grandma Rowan promises to send him a drawing of Biscuit every month. Birimo's rain cloud disappears, and for the first time, the sky over the highlands is completely clear. Now, phonics. Let's review. Confused has one f. Work out means end well, and everything worked out in the end. I'm so sorry is said low and soft. Under the weather means a little sick. Courageous keeps the e in courage. Next time, it's the Heart Festival on Heart Hill!

lessons.teacherScript: Hello, everyone! Last time, we said, That must be hard for you. I should have noticed sooner. Today is the Heart Festival on Heart Hill! The whole village climbs the hill together. Grandma Rowan walks with Biscuit, Mr. Bram carries a basket of scones, and Finn holds hands with his new friend Ellie. Under the Great Rainbow, villagers take turns sharing their feelings. A boy says he was annoyed when his kite got stuck in a tree, but he turned to his big sister, and she helped him get it down. A farmer says he is on cloud nine, because a new lamb was born this morning. Everyone shouts, Congratulations! Then I ask everyone to share what we learned. Kiko steps forward and says, Words can heal hearts. Say it with me. Words can heal hearts. Wonderful! Let's read Kiko's speech. "When we came to the highlands, the Great Rainbow had no colors, because people had stopped sharing their feelings. Here, we learned that it's OK to feel sad, nervous or annoyed. We learned to listen and say, That must be hard. We learned to say sorry and to make up after a fight. We learned to persuade with kind reasons, and to ask questions that help people tell their stories. Most of all, we learned that words can heal hearts. A kind word can chase away a rain cloud. A sorry can clear the fog. A thank you can bring out the sun. So please, keep asking each other, How are you really feeling? Thank you, Heatherbrook!" Why did the rainbow have no colors? Because people had stopped sharing their feelings. What can a sorry do? It can clear the fog. Everyone claps. And then the purple stripe comes back to the Great Rainbow! Red, orange, yellow, green, blue and purple. The rainbow is complete with six colors, and it shines over the whole highlands. Puff glows every color at once. At the very top of the hill, above the clouds, we see a huge hall. Inside, there is a big round table, and children from every continent are gathering around it. Who are they? Now, phonics. Let's review. Annoyed has double n. Turn to means go to someone for help. Congratulations goes high, then down. On cloud nine means very happy. Helpful ends in -ful. Thank you, Puff! Thank you, Grandma Rowan! Goodbye, Highlands of the Heart!
